theory.intro: The **derivative** $f'(x)$ is the gradient of the tangent to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x, f(x))$. It gives the instantaneous rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$.
facts: The derivative of $y=f(x)$ is written $f'(x)$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ or $y'$, and equals $\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
The gradient of the **secant line** through $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$ is the **average rate of change** $\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ over $[a, b]$.
The gradient of the **tangent line** at $x=a$ is the **instantaneous rate of change** there, written $f'(a)$.
The derivative exists at $x=a$ only where the tangent exists and is not vertical, so it fails at sharp corners, vertical tangents and discontinuities.

foundation.question_text: The tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $(3, 5)$ passes through $(5, 11)$. Find the value of $f'(3)$.
The equation of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=2$ is $y=4x-1$. State the value of $f'(2)$.
State whether the gradient of the secant line between $x=1$ and $x=5$ on a distance-time graph represents average speed or instantaneous speed.
foundation.solution_text: A secant line between two distinct points represents the average speed over that interval.

foundation.question_text: Name the geometric line whose gradient gives the instantaneous rate of change of a curve at a single point $x=a$.
foundation.solution_text: The tangent line to the curve at $x=a$.

foundation.question_text: Write the formal limit definition of the derivative $f'(x)$ in terms of $h$.
State what the notation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ represents in differential calculus.
foundation.solution_text: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ represents the derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ (the gradient function).

foundation.question_text: Explain why the absolute value function $f(x)=|x|$ does not have a derivative at $x=0$.
foundation.solution_text:
The graph has a sharp corner (v-shape) at $x=0$.
The gradient abruptly changes from $-1$ to $+1$, so no unique tangent line exists at $x=0$.

foundation.question_text: Does the derivative $f'(a)$ exist if the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=a$ is vertical? Justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text: No. A vertical line has an undefined (infinite) gradient, so $f'(a)$ does not exist.

development.question_text: A tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=-1$ passes through $(-1, 4)$ and $(2, -2)$. Calculate $f'(-1)$.
The tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $(4, 7)$ forms an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with the positive $x$-axis. Find $f'(4)$.
For $f(x)=x^2$, calculate the average rate of change over $[1, 3]$ and compare it to the instantaneous rate of change at $x=2$ given $f'(x)=2x$.
development.solution_text:
Average rate over $[1, 3]$:
$\dfrac{f(3)-f(1)}{3-1}=\dfrac{9-1}{2}=\dfrac{8}{2}=4$
Instantaneous rate at $x=2$:
$f'(2)=2(2)=4$
Both the average rate over $[1, 3]$ and the instantaneous rate at $x=2$ are equal to $4$.

development.question_text: Describe how the secant line through $P(c, f(c))$ and $Q(c+h, f(c+h))$ relates to the tangent line at $P$ as $h\to 0$.
development.solution_text:
As $h\to 0$, point $Q$ approaches point $P$ along the curve.
The secant line rotates and in the limit becomes the tangent line to the curve at $P$.

development.question_text: Express the instantaneous rate of change of volume $V$ with respect to radius $r$ at $r=a$ using limit notation.
Which of $f'(x)$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, and $y'$ are valid notations for the derived function of $y=f(x)$?
development.solution_text: All three notations ($f'(x)$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, and $y'$) are standard and valid representations of the derivative.

development.question_text: The graph of $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ has a vertical tangent at $(0, 0)$. State whether $f'(0)$ exists.
development.solution_text:
Because the tangent line at $(0, 0)$ is vertical (the $y$-axis), its gradient is undefined.
Therefore $f'(0)$ does not exist.

development.question_text: If a function $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x=3$, explain why $f'(3)$ does not exist.
development.solution_text:
A function must be continuous at a point to be differentiable.
Because of the jump discontinuity, the difference quotient does not approach a single finite limit as $h\to 0$.

mastery.question_text: The tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=3$ passes through $(1, 2)$ and $(5, 10)$. Find the equation of this tangent line and hence determine $f(3)$ and $f'(3)$.
mastery.solution_text:
Gradient $m=\dfrac{10-2}{5-1}=\dfrac{8}{4}=2$
Equation of tangent: $y-2=2(x-1) \implies y=2x$
At $x=3$:
$f(3)=2(3)=6$
$f'(3)=2$
$f(3)=6$ and $f'(3)=2$.

mastery.question_text: A particle moves with position $s(t)=t^2+t$ metres. Find the average velocity over $[2, 2+h]$ and show that its limit as $h\to 0$ gives $s'(2)=5$.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}$
$=\dfrac{[(2+h)^2+(2+h)]-[2^2+2]}{h}$
$=\dfrac{4+4h+h^2+2+h-6}{h}$
$=\dfrac{5h+h^2}{h}$
$=5+h$
As $h\to 0$, average velocity approaches $5\text{ m/s}$, so $s'(2)=5$.

mastery.question_text: Consider the piecewise function $f(x)=\begin{cases} 2x & \text{for } x \le 1 \\ x^2+1 & \text{for } x > 1 \end{cases}$. Determine whether $f'(1)$ exists by evaluating the left-hand and right-hand gradients at $x=1$.
mastery.solution_text:
Left-hand derivative: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(2x)=2$
Right-hand derivative: $\lim_{h\to 0^+}\dfrac{(1+h)^2+1-2}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^+}\dfrac{2h+h^2}{h}=2$
Both left and right gradients equal $2$, and $f(1)=2$ is continuous.
$f'(1)=2$ exists.
